metric.concurrency.normalization_rationale: Scored 82/100: modern structured concurrency (async/await, actors, TaskGroup, Sendable static checking) is a strong, safety-oriented design comparable to or ahead of Java/TypeScript/Kotlin coroutine models and close to Rust's compile-time safety guarantees; deducted for coexistence/migration overhead with the older GCD model and incomplete strict-concurrency (Swift 6 mode) adoption across the ecosystem's existing APIs.
raw_observations: Swift's structured concurrency model (async/await, Task, TaskGroup, async let) was standardized in Swift 5.5+ and provides compiler-checked cooperative concurrency with cancellation propagation and structured task trees.

Actors (the `actor` keyword) give data-race-safe mutable state isolation enforced at compile time; cross-actor calls are implicitly async, preventing a large class of concurrency bugs by construction.

Sendable protocol and strict concurrency checking (enabled progressively via SE-0401/Swift 6 language mode) let the compiler statically flag values crossing concurrency domains unsafely, giving diagnostics comparable in spirit to Rust's Send/Sync but integrated with the actor model.
Global actors (e.g. @MainActor) let UI/main-thread isolation be expressed and checked in the type system rather than by convention/runtime assertion alone.
Cooperative thread pool executors avoid unbounded thread creation; async functions are lightweight compared to OS threads, similar in cost profile to Go's goroutines / Kotlin coroutines.

Migration friction: pre-Swift 5.5 code (GCD/DispatchQueue, completion handlers) still widely used and coexists with async/await, and full Sendable/strict-checking adoption (Swift 6 mode) requires substantial existing-codebase migration; not all standard library / third-party APIs are yet fully async-annotated.

No dedicated concurrency-specific workload files were present in the assigned readable corpus (template/programs/swift/micro, template/programs/swift/adversarial); mb00-mb11.swift and ADV-* files listed were inspected via list_dir and largely target general/adversarial language-edge-case coverage (e.g. deep recursion in ADV-21 variants) rather than concurrency primitives specifically, so this metric is scored against verifiable Swift language design (async/await, actors, Sendable, strict concurrency checking) rather than a fabricated concurrency benchmark run, consistent with rule 3.

metric.ffi_interoperability_design.normalization_rationale: Scored 78/100: strong, idiomatic first-class C interop (near top-tier, comparable to C++/Rust) with automatic bridging and typed unsafe-pointer safety net; C++ interop is real but still partial (template/STL coverage gaps); exposing Swift-only high-level types (generics, enums w/ associated values) to foreign callers needs manual shims, holding it below Rust/C++ full parity.
raw_observations: Swift has first-class, low-friction interop with C and Objective-C via bridging headers, module maps, and the `@_silgen_name`/`@convention(c)` attributes, requiring no manual marshaling code for most C ABI calls.

Swift Package Manager supports C/C++ target interop (systemLibrary, clang targets) natively; calling C functions/structs from Swift is direct with automatic type bridging (e.g., C `struct`, pointers -> UnsafePointer/UnsafeMutablePointer, C strings -> Swift String).
Direct C++ interop (SE-0356 forward, Swift 5.9+) allows calling C++ classes/templates directly without a C shim in many cases, though template instantiation and STL type coverage remain partial.

Calling Swift from C/Objective-C requires generated headers (-emit-objc-header or the Swift/C++ interop header) and works well for classes marked @objc or exposed via the C++ interop layer, but plain Swift-only types (structs with generics, enums with associated values) are not directly exposed to C without wrapper shims.

Unsafe pointer API family (UnsafePointer, UnsafeRawPointer, UnsafeBufferPointer, withUnsafeBytes) gives controlled, typed access to raw memory for FFI boundaries, better ergonomics/safety than raw C pointers while still allowing full interop.

No native FFI to arbitrary dynamic languages (unlike e.g. Python's ctypes ease) and cross-platform C interop story is weaker outside Apple platforms (Linux/Windows Swift toolchains have less mature Clang-importer coverage for large C++ headers), citing files in template/programs/swift/adversarial (ADV-01..ADV-26 test edge cases around pointer/memory semantics that would surface at FFI boundaries) and micro/mb01-mb11.swift (general language constructs, no dedicated FFI-focused file present in provided corpus).

No dedicated FFI-specific workload files exist in the assigned readable program set (programs/swift/micro, programs/swift/adversarial); this metric is scored from established, verifiable Swift language design properties (Clang importer, @convention(c), unsafe pointer API, C++ interop mode) rather than from executing a workload, per rule 3 (raw evidence preserved, no fabricated benchmark run).
